title: Why Do Bullet Trains Have Such Long Noses?
description:
The nose of a Japanese bullet train can be longer than a whole subway car. On some trains, a big part of the first car is just nose, with no seats inside. That looks like a waste of space on the most crowded railway in the world. But without that nose, every time the train entered a tunnel, people living near the exit would hear a bang like a cannon. Today, ten parts of the bullet train, and why each one exists.

Machine Reverse takes apart the machines you see every day and explains, part by part, why each one exists. This video covers 10 parts.

Chapters:
0:00 Intro
1:20 1. The long nose
2:48 2. The tunnel hood
4:08 3. The owl pantograph
5:31 4. The sealed body
6:57 5. The tilting body
8:22 6. The snow sprinklers
9:40 7. The track without stones
11:01 8. The earthquake detectors
12:50 9. The yellow train
14:08 10. The wider track
15:35 The verdict

Sources:
- Tokaido Shinkansen opening (1 Oct 1964), punctuality and safety record: JR Central, "About the Shinkansen" https://global.jr-central.co.jp/en/company/about_shinkansen/ and Wikipedia, "Shinkansen" https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shinkansen
- Tunnel boom (micro-pressure waves) and nose length: Wikipedia, "Tunnel boom" https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tunnel_boom
- Kingfisher nose and owl-inspired pantograph (Eiji Nakatsu, 500 series): Wikipedia, "500 Series Shinkansen" https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/500_Series_Shinkansen and Ask Nature, "Shinkansen train" https://asknature.org/innovation/high-speed-train-inspired-by-the-kingfisher/
- ALFA-X (22 m nose): Wikipedia, "ALFA-X" https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ALFA-X
- N700 series body tilting (1 degree, 270 km/h on 2,500 m curves): Wikipedia, "N700 Series Shinkansen" https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/N700_Series_Shinkansen
- Snow countermeasures at Sekigahara: JR Central, "Snow countermeasures" https://global.jr-central.co.jp/en/
- Slab track on the Sanyo Shinkansen: Wikipedia, "Slab track" https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ballastless_track
- Earthquake detection (UrEDAS) and the 2004 Chuetsu derailment: Wikipedia, "Urgent Earthquake Detection and Alarm System" https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UrEDAS and "Jōetsu Shinkansen" https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/J%C5%8Detsu_Shinkansen
- Shinkansen during the 2011 Tohoku earthquake: Wikipedia, "Tōhoku Shinkansen" https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/T%C5%8Dhoku_Shinkansen
- Doctor Yellow and its retirement (JR Central, January 2025): Wikipedia, "Doctor Yellow" https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doctor_Yellow
- Gauge (1,067 mm vs 1,435 mm) and mini-Shinkansen: Wikipedia, "Mini-shinkansen" https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mini-shinkansen
